1→# Discrete Stochastic Simulation Solver
     2→
     3→This repository contains a Julia implementation of a discrete stochastic simulation solver. It provides examples based on the Chemical Master Equation (CME) in the `examples/` directory, along with code to reproduce the figures from our paper.
     4→
     5→## Overview
     6→
     7→The solver is designed for simulating the time evolution of probability distributions over the state space in discrete stochastic systems. In the context of chemical reaction networks, it approximates the **Chemical Master Equation (CME)**:
     8→
     9→$$
    10→\frac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{p}(t) = \mathbf{A}\,\boldsymbol{p}(t),
    11→$$
    12→
    13→where \(\boldsymbol{p}(t)\) is the probability vector and \(\mathbf{A}\) is the generator matrix. Due to the typically infinite state space, the solver works on a truncated state space and carefully controls the error introduced by the truncation.
    14→
    15→### Quantile-Based Pruning
    16→
    17→At each time step, the algorithm prunes a fixed fraction \(\alpha\) of the states with the smallest probabilities by:
    18→
    19→1. **Sorting states by probability.**
    20→2. **Computing the cumulative probability:**
    21→
    22→   $$
    23→   P_{\mathrm{cumulative}}(k,t) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} p(x_i,t)
    24→   $$
    25→
    26→3. **Determining the cutoff index \(k^*\):**  
    27→   \(k^*\) is chosen such that 
    28→   
    29→   $$
    30→   P_{\mathrm{cumulative}}(k^*,t) \ge \alpha \quad \text{and} \quad P_{\mathrm{cumulative}}(k^*-1,t) < \alpha.
    31→   $$
    32→   
    33→   The cutoff probability \(q_\alpha = p(x_{k^*},t)\) is then used to remove all states with probabilities \(\le q_\alpha\).
    34→
    35→After pruning, the remaining probability mass is renormalized so that the new probability vector sums to one. Theoretical analysis shows that if the total pruned mass is \(m\), then the error in the \(\ell^1\)-norm is bounded by
    36→
    37→$$
    38→\|\boldsymbol{p}(t)-\widetilde{\boldsymbol{p}}(t)\|_1 \le 2\,m.
    39→$$
    40→
    41→### Error Control and Adaptive Time Stepping
    42→
    43→The solver employs an adaptive time-stepping rule to ensure the local error per step—accounting for both the truncation error and the time-stepping error from approximating the matrix exponential—remains within a prescribed tolerance. The adaptive step size is determined by an inequality of the form
    44→
    45→$$
    46→\delta t \le \left(\frac{\epsilon_{\mathrm{tol}} - \epsilon_{\mathrm{trunc}}(t)}{C}\right)^{\!1/p},
    47→$$
    48→
    49→where \(C\) and \(p\) are constants derived from the error analysis.
    50→
    51→## Usage
    52→
    53→Detailed examples are available in the `examples/` directory.
    54→
    55→
    56→[![Stable](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-stable-blue.svg)](https://AdityaDendukuri.github.io/DiscStochSim.jl/stable/)
    57→[![Dev](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-dev-blue.svg)](https://AdityaDendukuri.github.io/DiscStochSim.jl/dev/)
    58→[![Build Status](https://github.com/AdityaDendukuri/DiscStochSim.jl/actions/workflows/CI.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/AdityaDendukuri/DiscStochSim.jl/actions/workflows/CI.yml?query=branch%3Amain)
    59→[![Coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/AdityaDendukuri/DiscStochSim.jl/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/AdityaDendukuri/DiscStochSim.jl)

1→"""
     2→    DiscreteStochasticSystem{E}
     3→
     4→A discrete stochastic system with stoichiometric vectors and propensity functions,
     5→constructed from a Catalyst `ReactionSystem`.
     6→
     7→# Fields
     8→- `stoichvecs::Vector{E}`: Net stoichiometric change vectors (one per reaction).
     9→- `propensities::Vector{Function}`: Propensity functions `(state, rates, t) -> α`.
    10→"""
    11→struct DiscreteStochasticSystem{E}
    12→    stoichvecs::Vector{E}
    13→    propensities::Vector{Function}
    14→end
    15→
    16→"""
    17→    DiscreteStochasticSystem(rn::ReactionSystem)
    18→
    19→Construct a `DiscreteStochasticSystem` from a Catalyst `ReactionSystem`.
    20→Stoichiometric vectors are stored as `CartesianIndex`, and propensity functions
    21→are built via `Catalyst.jumpratelaw` + `build_function`.
    22→"""
    23→function DiscreteStochasticSystem(rn::ReactionSystem)
    24→    X = Catalyst.get_species(rn)
    25→    P = Catalyst.get_ps(rn)
    26→
    27→    stoichvecs = map(eachcol(netstoichmat(rn))) do col
    28→        CartesianIndex(col...)
    29→    end
    30→
    31→    propensities = map(Catalyst.get_rxs(rn)) do rx
    32→        eqn = jumpratelaw(rx; combinatoric_ratelaw=true)
    33→        build_function(eqn, X, P, expression=Val{false})
    34→    end
    35→
    36→    DiscreteStochasticSystem{CartesianIndex}(stoichvecs, propensities)
    37→end
    38→

1→"""
     2→    StateSpace{E, T<:Real}
     3→
     4→Tracks active states, their probabilities, and a stable global ID mapping.
     5→
     6→- `states[i]` is the i-th active state.
     7→- `probs[i]`  is its probability.
     8→- `index[x]`  gives the compact position of state `x` in `states`.
     9→- `global_id[x]` gives the permanent ID assigned when `x` was first added.
    10→- `id_to_state[id]` maps permanent ID back to state (append-only).
    11→- `next_id` is the next global ID to assign.
    12→"""
    13→mutable struct StateSpace{E, T<:Real}
    14→    states::Vector{E}
    15→    probs::Vector{T}
    16→    index::Dict{E,Int}
    17→    global_id::Dict{E,Int}
    18→    id_to_state::Vector{E}
    19→    next_id::Int
    20→end
    21→
    22→function StateSpace{E,T}() where {E,T<:Real}
    23→    StateSpace{E,T}(E[], T[], Dict{E,Int}(), Dict{E,Int}(), E[], 1)
    24→end
    25→
    26→Base.length(sp::StateSpace) = length(sp.states)
    27→
    28→"""
    29→    add_state!(space, state, prob=0.0)
    30→
    31→Add `state` with probability `prob`. No-op if already present. O(1).
    32→"""
    33→function add_state!(sp::StateSpace{E,T}, state::E, prob::T=zero(T)) where {E,T}
    34→    haskey(sp.index, state) && return sp
    35→    push!(sp.states, state)
    36→    push!(sp.probs, prob)
    37→    sp.index[state] = length(sp.states)
    38→    if !haskey(sp.global_id, state)
    39→        sp.global_id[state] = sp.next_id
    40→        push!(sp.id_to_state, state)
    41→        sp.next_id += 1
    42→    end
    43→    sp
    44→end
    45→
    46→"""
    47→    remove_states!(space, mask)
    48→
    49→Remove states where `mask[i] == true`. Rebuild compact index.
    50→"""
    51→function remove_states!(sp::StateSpace{E,T}, remove_mask::BitVector) where {E,T}
    52→    keep = .!remove_mask
    53→    sp.states = sp.states[keep]
    54→    sp.probs = sp.probs[keep]
    55→    empty!(sp.index)
    56→    for (i, s) in enumerate(sp.states)
    57→        sp.index[s] = i
    58→    end
    59→    sp
    60→end
    61→
    62→"""
    63→    expand!(space, model, bc; depth=1)
    64→
    65→Add stoichiometric neighbors of all current states that satisfy `bc`.
    66→Probabilities of new states are initialized to zero.
    67→"""
    68→function expand!(sp::StateSpace{E,T}, model, bc; depth::Int=1) where {E,T}
    69→    for _ in 1:depth
    70→        current = copy(sp.states)
    71→        for x in current
    72→            for ν in model.stoichvecs
    73→                y = x + ν
    74→                if !haskey(sp.index, y) && bc(y)
    75→                    add_state!(sp, y)
    76→                end
    77→            end
    78→        end
    79→    end
    80→    sp
    81→end
    82→
    83→"""
    84→    expand_ssa!(space, model, rates, t, bc; depth=1)
    85→
    86→Legacy SSA-style expansion: for each active state, sample one reaction by
    87→propensity and add the sampled successor if it satisfies `bc`.
    88→"""
    89→function expand_ssa!(sp::StateSpace{E,T}, model, rates, t::Real, bc; depth::Int=1) where {E,T}
    90→    n_rxn = length(model.stoichvecs)
    91→    n_rxn == 0 && return sp
    92→
    93→    for _ in 1:depth
    94→        current = copy(sp.states)
    95→        for x in current
    96→            props = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_rxn)
    97→            total = 0.0
    98→            @inbounds for k in 1:n_rxn
    99→                α = Float64(model.propensities[k](x, rates, t))
   100→                α = max(0.0, α)
   101→                props[k] = α
   102→                total += α
   103→            end
   104→            total <= 0 && continue
   105→
   106→            threshold = rand() * total
   107→            csum = 0.0
   108→            chosen = 0
   109→            @inbounds for k in 1:n_rxn
   110→                csum += props[k]
   111→                if threshold <= csum
   112→                    chosen = k
   113→                    break
   114→                end
   115→            end
   116→            chosen == 0 && continue
   117→
   118→            y = x + model.stoichvecs[chosen]
   119→            if !haskey(sp.index, y) && bc(y)
   120→                add_state!(sp, y)
   121→            end
   122→        end
   123→    end
   124→    sp
   125→end
   126→
   127→"""
   128→    compress!(space, model, rates, t, prob_quantile; flux_tolerance=1e-6)
   129→
   130→Flux-aware pruning with legacy count-quantile candidate selection.
   131→
   132→Candidates are chosen by state count:
   133→`round(prob_quantile * n_states)` lowest-probability states.
   134→If `flux_tolerance <= 0`, all candidates are pruned.
   135→Returns `(total_flux, n_removed)`.
   136→"""
   137→function compress!(sp::StateSpace{E,T}, model, rates, t::Real,
   138→                   prob_quantile::Real; flux_tolerance::Real=1e-6) where {E,T}
   139→    n = length(sp)
   140→    n == 0 && return (zero(T), 0)
   141→
   142→    # Compute flux for each state: p(x) * sum_k a_k(x)
   143→    flux = Vector{T}(undef, n)
   144→    @inbounds for i in 1:n
   145→        w = zero(T)
   146→        for prop in model.propensities
   147→            w += prop(sp.states[i], rates, t)
   148→        end
   149→        flux[i] = sp.probs[i] * w
   150→    end
   151→    total_flux = sum(flux)
   152→    flux_threshold = total_flux * flux_tolerance
   153→
   154→    idx = sortperm(sp.probs)
   155→    n_remove = round(Int, clamp(prob_quantile, 0, 1) * n)
   156→    candidates = n_remove > 0 ? idx[1:min(n_remove, n)] : Int[]
   157→
   158→    remove_mask = falses(n)
   159→    n_removed = 0
   160→    if flux_tolerance <= 0
   161→        for i in candidates
   162→            remove_mask[i] = true
   163→            n_removed += 1
   164→        end
   165→    else
   166→        for i in candidates
   167→            if flux[i] < flux_threshold
   168→                remove_mask[i] = true
   169→                n_removed += 1
   170→            end
   171→        end
   172→    end
   173→
   174→    remove_states!(sp, remove_mask)
   175→    (total_flux, n_removed)
   176→end
   177→
   178→"""
   179→    renormalize!(space)
   180→
   181→Scale probabilities so they sum to 1. Returns the sum before normalization.
   182→"""
   183→function renormalize!(sp::StateSpace)
   184→    s = sum(sp.probs)
   185→    if s > 0
   186→        sp.probs ./= s
   187→    end
   188→    s
   189→end
   190→
   191→"""
   192→    get_global_ids(space) -> Vector{Int}
   193→
   194→Return the global IDs of the current active states (in compact order).
   195→"""
   196→function get_global_ids(sp::StateSpace)
   197→    [sp.global_id[s] for s in sp.states]
   198→end
   199→

1→"""
     2→    build_generator(space, model, rates, t) -> (A, in_flow, out_flow)
     3→
     4→Build the CME generator matrix from scratch in CSC-friendly COO format.
     5→
     6→For each column j (state x_j), iterate over reactions k with stoich vector ν_k:
     7→  - Off-diagonal: A[i,j] += a_k(x_j) where x_j + ν_k = x_i ∈ active set
     8→  - Diagonal:     A[j,j]  = -sum of off-diagonal column entries
     9→
    10→Returns `(A, in_flow, out_flow)` where `A = in_flow + out_flow`,
    11→`out_flow = diag(A)` (negative), `in_flow = A - out_flow` (non-negative).
    12→"""
    13→function build_generator(sp::StateSpace{E,T}, model, rates, t::Real) where {E,T}
    14→    n = length(sp)
    15→    n == 0 && return (spzeros(T, 0, 0), spzeros(T, 0, 0), spzeros(T, 0, 0))
    16→
    17→    # Pre-estimate nnz: at most n_reactions off-diagonal entries per column + 1 diagonal
    18→    n_rxn = length(model.stoichvecs)
    19→    sizehint = n * (n_rxn + 1)
    20→    I = Vector{Int}(); J = Vector{Int}(); V = Vector{T}()
    21→    sizehint!(I, sizehint); sizehint!(J, sizehint); sizehint!(V, sizehint)
    22→
    23→    @inbounds for j in 1:n
    24→        x = sp.states[j]
    25→        col_sum = zero(T)
    26→
    27→        for k in 1:n_rxn
    28→            y = x + model.stoichvecs[k]
    29→            i = get(sp.index, y, 0)
    30→            if i != 0
    31→                α = convert(T, model.propensities[k](x, rates, t))
    32→                if α > 0
    33→                    push!(I, i); push!(J, j); push!(V, α)
    34→                    col_sum += α
    35→                end
    36→            end
    37→        end
    38→
    39→        if col_sum > 0
    40→            push!(I, j); push!(J, j); push!(V, -col_sum)
    41→        end
    42→    end
    43→
    44→    A = sparse(I, J, V, n, n)
    45→    out_flow = spdiagm(0 => diag(A))
    46→    in_flow = A - out_flow
    47→    (A, in_flow, out_flow)
    48→end
    49→
    50→"""
    51→    reconstruct_generator(sp, model, rates, t, A_old, gids_old) -> (A, in_flow, out_flow)
    52→
    53→Incremental rebuild: reuse columns from `A_old` for states that were present in the
    54→previous step (matched via global IDs). Build new columns from scratch.
    55→
    56→Falls back to `build_generator` if overlap is below 30%.
    57→"""
    58→function reconstruct_generator(sp::StateSpace{E,T}, model, rates, t::Real,
    59→                               A_old::SparseMatrixCSC, gids_old::Vector{Int}) where {E,T}
    60→    n_new = length(sp)
    61→    n_new == 0 && return build_generator(sp, model, rates, t)
    62→
    63→    gids_new = get_global_ids(sp)
    64→
    65→    # Map old global ID → old column index
    66→    old_gid_to_col = Dict{Int,Int}()
    67→    for (col, gid) in enumerate(gids_old)
    68→        old_gid_to_col[gid] = col
    69→    end
    70→
    71→    # Count retained columns
    72→    n_retained = count(gid -> haskey(old_gid_to_col, gid), gids_new)
    73→    if n_retained < 0.3 * n_new
    74→        return build_generator(sp, model, rates, t)
    75→    end
    76→
    77→    # Build new-row-index lookup for all active states (by global ID)
    78→    gid_to_new_row = Dict{Int,Int}()
    79→    for (row, gid) in enumerate(gids_new)
    80→        gid_to_new_row[gid] = row
    81→    end
    82→
    83→    # Old global ID → old row index
    84→    old_gid_to_row = Dict{Int,Int}()
    85→    for (row, gid) in enumerate(gids_old)
    86→        old_gid_to_row[gid] = row
    87→    end
    88→
    89→    n_rxn = length(model.stoichvecs)
    90→    sizehint_n = n_new * (n_rxn + 1)
    91→    I = Vector{Int}(); J = Vector{Int}(); V = Vector{T}()
    92→    sizehint!(I, sizehint_n); sizehint!(J, sizehint_n); sizehint!(V, sizehint_n)
    93→
    94→    @inbounds for (j_new, gid) in enumerate(gids_new)
    95→        old_col = get(old_gid_to_col, gid, 0)
    96→
    97→        if old_col != 0
    98→            # Retained column: copy old off-diagonal entries + add new neighbors
    99→            x = sp.states[j_new]
   100→            col_sum = zero(T)
   101→
   102→            # Collect old off-diagonal targets (by new row index) for dedup
   103→            old_targets = Set{Int}()
   104→            for idx in nzrange(A_old, old_col)
   105→                old_row = A_old.rowval[idx]
   106→                old_row == old_col && continue  # skip diagonal
   107→                val = A_old.nzval[idx]
   108→                old_row_gid = gids_old[old_row]
   109→                new_row = get(gid_to_new_row, old_row_gid, 0)
   110→                if new_row != 0
   111→                    push!(I, new_row); push!(J, j_new); push!(V, val)
   112→                    col_sum += val
   113→                    push!(old_targets, new_row)
   114→                end
   115→            end
   116→
   117→            # Check for NEW neighbors not in old state space
   118→            for k in 1:n_rxn
   119→                y = x + model.stoichvecs[k]
   120→                i_new = get(sp.index, y, 0)
   121→                if i_new != 0 && i_new != j_new && !(i_new in old_targets)
   122→                    # This neighbor is new — compute propensity
   123→                    α = convert(T, model.propensities[k](x, rates, t))
   124→                    if α > 0
   125→                        push!(I, i_new); push!(J, j_new); push!(V, α)
   126→                        col_sum += α
   127→                    end
   128→                end
   129→            end
   130→
   131→            if col_sum > 0
   132→                push!(I, j_new); push!(J, j_new); push!(V, -col_sum)
   133→            end
   134→        else
   135→            # New column: build from scratch
   136→            x = sp.states[j_new]
   137→            col_sum = zero(T)
   138→            for k in 1:n_rxn
   139→                y = x + model.stoichvecs[k]
   140→                i_new = get(sp.index, y, 0)
   141→                if i_new != 0
   142→                    α = convert(T, model.propensities[k](x, rates, t))
   143→                    if α > 0
   144→                        push!(I, i_new); push!(J, j_new); push!(V, α)
   145→                        col_sum += α
   146→                    end
   147→                end
   148→            end
   149→            if col_sum > 0
   150→                push!(I, j_new); push!(J, j_new); push!(V, -col_sum)
   151→            end
   152→        end
   153→    end
   154→
   155→    A = sparse(I, J, V, n_new, n_new)
   156→    out_flow = spdiagm(0 => diag(A))
   157→    in_flow = A - out_flow
   158→    (A, in_flow, out_flow)
   159→end
   160→

1→"""
     2→    FSPProblem(rn, u0, tspan, rates; bounds=(0, 50_000))
     3→
     4→Defines a Chemical Master Equation problem for the Finite State Projection method.
     5→
     6→# Arguments
     7→- `rn::ReactionSystem`: Catalyst reaction network.
     8→- `u0::CartesianIndex`: Initial state.
     9→- `tspan::Tuple{Real,Real}`: Time interval `(t0, tf)`.
    10→- `rates::Vector`: Reaction rate parameters.
    11→- `bounds`: Domain bounds passed to `RectLatticeBoundaryCondition`.
    12→"""
    13→struct FSPProblem{E, T<:Real}
    14→    model::DiscreteStochasticSystem{E}
    15→    u0::E
    16→    tspan::Tuple{T,T}
    17→    rates::Vector{T}
    18→    bc::Function
    19→end
    20→
    21→function FSPProblem(rn::ReactionSystem, u0::CartesianIndex, tspan::Tuple,
    22→                    rates::Vector; bounds=(0, 50_000))
    23→    model = DiscreteStochasticSystem(rn)
    24→    T = promote_type(eltype(rates), typeof(tspan[1]), typeof(tspan[2]))
    25→    tspan_T = (T(tspan[1]), T(tspan[2]))
    26→    rates_T = T.(rates)
    27→    bc = x -> RectLatticeBoundaryCondition(x, bounds)
    28→    FSPProblem{CartesianIndex, T}(model, u0, tspan_T, rates_T, bc)
    29→end

1→"""
     2→    FSPSolution
     3→
     4→Stores snapshots from an adaptive FSP solve.
     5→
     6→# Fields
     7→- `t::Vector{Float64}`: Time points of saved snapshots.
     8→- `snapshots::Vector{Tuple{Vector{E}, Vector{Float64}}}`: `(states, probs)` at each snapshot.
     9→- `state_space_sizes::Vector{Int}`: State space size at each snapshot.
    10→- `n_species::Int`: Number of species (dimension of CartesianIndex).
    11→"""
    12→struct FSPSolution{E}
    13→    t::Vector{Float64}
    14→    snapshots::Vector{Tuple{Vector{E}, Vector{Float64}}}
    15→    state_space_sizes::Vector{Int}
    16→    n_species::Int
    17→end
    18→
    19→Base.length(sol::FSPSolution) = length(sol.t)
    20→
    21→"""
    22→    sol[i] -> (states, probs)
    23→
    24→Return the i-th snapshot.
    25→"""
    26→Base.getindex(sol::FSPSolution, i::Int) = sol.snapshots[i]
    27→
    28→"""
    29→    mean_trajectory(sol) -> Matrix{Float64}
    30→
    31→Compute the mean state at each snapshot. Returns an `n_snapshots × n_species` matrix.
    32→"""
    33→function mean_trajectory(sol::FSPSolution)
    34→    ns = sol.n_species
    35→    nt = length(sol)
    36→    result = zeros(nt, ns)
    37→    for i in 1:nt
    38→        states, probs = sol.snapshots[i]
    39→        for (s, p) in zip(states, probs)
    40→            for d in 1:ns
    41→                result[i, d] += s[d] * p
    42→            end
    43→        end
    44→    end
    45→    result
    46→end
    47→
    48→"""
    49→    marginal(sol, i, species) -> (values, probs)
    50→
    51→Compute the marginal distribution of `species` (1-indexed) at snapshot `i`.
    52→Returns sorted `(values, probs)` vectors.
    53→"""
    54→function marginal(sol::FSPSolution, i::Int, species::Int)
    55→    states, probs = sol.snapshots[i]
    56→    dist = Dict{Int, Float64}()
    57→    for (s, p) in zip(states, probs)
    58→        v = s[species]
    59→        dist[v] = get(dist, v, 0.0) + p
    60→    end
    61→    vals = sort(collect(keys(dist)))
    62→    ps = [dist[v] for v in vals]
    63→    (values=vals, probs=ps)
    64→end
    65→

1→"""
     2→    AdaptiveFSP(; kwargs...)
     3→
     4→Algorithm parameters for the adaptive Finite State Projection method.
     5→
     6→# Keyword Arguments
     7→- `ε_dt::Float64 = 1.0`: Time-step control: `dt = ε_dt / total_flux`.
     8→- `prob_quantile::Float64 = 0.1`: Quantile parameter used by pruning.
     9→- `flux_tolerance::Float64 = 1e-6`: Flux protection threshold (relative to total flux).
    10→- `expansion_depth::Int = 1`: Number of neighbor shells added per step.
    11→- `save_interval::Int = 1000`: Save a snapshot every N iterations.
    12→"""
    13→Base.@kwdef struct AdaptiveFSP
    14→    ε_dt::Float64 = 1.0
    15→    prob_quantile::Float64 = 0.1
    16→    flux_tolerance::Float64 = 1e-6
    17→    expansion_depth::Int = 1
    18→    save_interval::Int = 1000
    19→end
    20→
    21→"""
    22→    solve(prob::FSPProblem, alg::AdaptiveFSP) -> FSPSolution
    23→
    24→Run the adaptive FSP algorithm:
    25→1. Expand state space (stoichiometric neighbors).
    26→2. Build the CME generator.
    27→3. Compute adaptive time step from boundary flux.
    28→4. Propagate probability via matrix exponential (`expv`).
    29→5. Flux-aware pruning + renormalization.
    30→6. Repeat until `t >= tf`.
    31→"""
    32→function CommonSolve.solve(prob::FSPProblem{E,T}, alg::AdaptiveFSP) where {E,T}
    33→    model = prob.model
    34→    rates = prob.rates
    35→    bc = prob.bc
    36→    t0, tf = prob.tspan
    37→    n_species = length(Tuple(prob.u0))
    38→
    39→    # Initialize state space
    40→    sp = StateSpace{E, Float64}()
    41→    add_state!(sp, prob.u0, 1.0)
    42→
    43→    # Solution storage
    44→    sol_t = Float64[t0]
    45→    sol_snaps = [(copy(sp.states), copy(sp.probs))]
    46→    sol_sizes = [length(sp)]
    47→
    48→    t = Float64(t0)
    49→    iter = 0
    50→
    51→    while t < tf
    52→        iter += 1
    53→
    54→        # 1) Expand state space (legacy SSA-style expansion)
    55→        expand_ssa!(sp, model, rates, t, bc; depth=alg.expansion_depth)
    56→
    57→        # 2) Build generator from scratch (legacy behavior)
    58→        A, in_flow, out_flow = build_generator(sp, model, rates, t)
    59→
    60→        # 3) Adaptive time step from total outflux
    61→        out_flux = Vector(-out_flow * sp.probs)
    62→        total_flux = sum(out_flux)
    63→        dt = total_flux > 0 ? alg.ε_dt / total_flux : (tf - t)
    64→        dt = min(dt, tf - t)
    65→
    66→        # 4) Propagate probability
    67→        sp.probs = expmv(dt, A, sp.probs)
    68→
    69→        # 5) Flux-aware pruning + renormalization
    70→        compress!(sp, model, rates, t, alg.prob_quantile;
    71→                  flux_tolerance=alg.flux_tolerance)
    72→        renormalize!(sp)
    73→
    74→        # 7) Advance time
    75→        t += dt
    76→
    77→        # 8) Save snapshot
    78→        if iter % alg.save_interval == 0 || t >= tf
    79→            push!(sol_t, t)
    80→            push!(sol_snaps, (copy(sp.states), copy(sp.probs)))
    81→            push!(sol_sizes, length(sp))
    82→            @info "t = $(round(t; sigdigits=4)), |S| = $(length(sp)), dt = $(round(dt; sigdigits=3))"
    83→        end
    84→    end
    85→
    86→    # Ensure final snapshot is captured
    87→    if sol_t[end] < t
    88→        push!(sol_t, t)
    89→        push!(sol_snaps, (copy(sp.states), copy(sp.probs)))
    90→        push!(sol_sizes, length(sp))
    91→    end
    92→
    93→    FSPSolution{E}(sol_t, sol_snaps, sol_sizes, n_species)
    94→end
    95→

1→using DiscStochSim
     2→using Catalyst
     3→using Random
     4→using Plots
     5→
     6→const OREGONATOR_FACE = RGB(0.92, 0.92, 0.92)
     7→
     8→function parse_tfinal(args; default::Float64=0.11)::Float64
     9→    isempty(args) && return default
    10→    try
    11→        parse(Float64, args[1])
    12→    catch
    13→        default
    14→    end
    15→end
    16→
    17→function oregonator_problem(; tfinal::Float64=0.11, bounds=(0, 50_000))
    18→    rn = @reaction_network begin
    19→        @species X(t) Y(t) Z(t)
    20→        @parameters k1 k2 k3 k4 k5
    21→        k1, Y --> X
    22→        k2, X + Y --> 0
    23→        k3, X --> 2X + Z
    24→        k4, 2X --> 0
    25→        k5, Z --> Y
    26→    end
    27→
    28→    y1s, y2s, y3s = 500.0, 1000.0, 2000.0
    29→    mu1s, mu2s = 2000.0, 50000.0
    30→    rates = [
    31→        mu1s / y2s,
    32→        mu2s / (y1s * y2s),
    33→        (mu1s + mu2s) / y1s,
    34→        2 * mu1s / y1s^2,
    35→        (mu1s + mu2s) / y3s,
    36→    ]
    37→
    38→    FSPProblem(rn, CartesianIndex(500, 1000, 2000), (0.0, tfinal), rates; bounds=bounds)
    39→end
    40→
    41→function solve_oregonator(; tfinal::Float64=0.11,
    42→                          ε_dt::Float64=1.0,
    43→                          prob_quantile::Float64=0.1,
    44→                          flux_tolerance::Float64=1.0,
    45→                          expansion_depth::Int=1,
    46→                          save_interval::Int=1000,
    47→                          seed::Int=1,
    48→                          bounds=(0, 50_000))
    49→    Random.seed!(seed)
    50→
    51→    prob = oregonator_problem(; tfinal=tfinal, bounds=bounds)
    52→    sol = solve(prob, AdaptiveFSP(
    53→        ε_dt=ε_dt,
    54→        prob_quantile=prob_quantile,
    55→        flux_tolerance=flux_tolerance,
    56→        expansion_depth=expansion_depth,
    57→        save_interval=save_interval,
    58→    ))
    59→
    60→    t = sol.t
    61→    dt = vcat([0.0], t[2:end] .- t[1:end-1])
    62→    traj = mean_trajectory(sol)
    63→
    64→    (
    65→        t = t,
    66→        dt = dt,
    67→        state_space_sizes = sol.state_space_sizes,
    68→        traj = traj,
    69→        sol = sol,
    70→    )
    71→end

1→# Bottleneck Paper Figures: flux_vs_naive_comparison.png + error_accumulation_analysis.png
     2→#
     3→# System: A →(k1) B, B →(k2) B+C
     4→# k1 = 1e-6, k2 = 0.1, initial state (1,0,0)
     5→#
     6→# Uses explicit FSP loops (not solve()) because the bottleneck system needs
     7→# small fixed time steps to track the wave front with incremental expansion.
     8→
     9→using DiscStochSim, Catalyst, CairoMakie, Expokit, SparseArrays, LinearAlgebra
    10→
    11→const N_SPECIES = 3
    12→
    13→# ============================================================================
    14→# Model definition
    15→# ============================================================================
    16→rn = @reaction_network begin
    17→    k1, A --> B
    18→    k2, B --> B + C
    19→end
    20→
    21→const MODEL = DiscreteStochasticSystem(rn)
    22→const RATES = [1e-6, 1e-1]
    23→const BC = x -> RectLatticeBoundaryCondition(x, (0, Int(1e11)))
    24→
    25→function compute_mean(sp::StateSpace)
    26→    μ = zeros(N_SPECIES)
    27→    for (i, s) in enumerate(sp.states)
    28→        for d in 1:N_SPECIES
    29→            μ[d] += s[d] * sp.probs[i]
    30→        end
    31→    end
    32→    μ
    33→end
    34→
    35→# ============================================================================
    36→# Simulation runners
    37→# ============================================================================
    38→function run_fsp(; δt, tf, prob_quantile, flux_tolerance, save_every, log_every)
    39→    sp = StateSpace{CartesianIndex{3}, Float64}()
    40→    add_state!(sp, CartesianIndex(1, 0, 0), 1.0)
    41→
    42→    n_steps = round(Int, tf / δt)
    43→    times = Float64[0.0]
    44→    means = zeros(1, N_SPECIES)
    45→    means[1, :] = compute_mean(sp)
    46→    sizes = Int[length(sp)]
    47→
    48→    gids_old = Int[]
    49→    A_old = spzeros(Float64, 0, 0)
    50→
    51→    for iter in 1:n_steps
    52→        t = iter * δt
    53→
    54→        expand!(sp, MODEL, BC; depth=1)
    55→
    56→        if isempty(gids_old)
    57→            A, _, _ = build_generator(sp, MODEL, RATES, t)
    58→        else
    59→            A, _, _ = reconstruct_generator(sp, MODEL, RATES, t, A_old, gids_old)
    60→        end
    61→
    62→        sp.probs = expmv(δt, A, sp.probs)
    63→
    64→        compress!(sp, MODEL, RATES, t, prob_quantile; flux_tolerance=flux_tolerance)
    65→        renormalize!(sp)
    66→
    67→        gids_old = get_global_ids(sp)
    68→        A_old = A
    69→
    70→        if iter % save_every == 0 || iter == n_steps
    71→            push!(times, t)
    72→            means = vcat(means, compute_mean(sp)')
    73→            push!(sizes, length(sp))
    74→        end
    75→
    76→        if iter % log_every == 0
    77→            μ = compute_mean(sp)
    78→            println("  t=$t, |S|=$(length(sp)), <A>=$(round(μ[1];sigdigits=3)), <C>=$(round(μ[3];sigdigits=4))")
    79→        end
    80→    end

#### **2. `/home/adiden/DiscStochSim.jl/src/state_space.jl`**
**Purpose**: Manages active state space and probability evolution

  - `remove_states!()`: Prune states based on mask
  - `expand!()`: Add stoichiometric neighbors within boundary
  - `expand_ssa!()`: SSA-style sampling-based expansion
  - `compress!()`: Flux-aware pruning (removes low-probability states while protecting active flow)
  - `renormalize!()`: Normalize probabilities to sum to 1
  - `get_global_ids()`: Retrieve stable IDs for reconstruction

#### **3. `/home/adiden/DiscStochSim.jl/src/boundary_conditions.jl`**
**Purpose**: Define valid state space domains
- `RectLatticeBoundaryCondition()`: Function checking if state is within rectangular bounds

**Purpose**: Construct CME generator matrix (key computational step)
- `build_generator()`: Build full generator matrix A from scratch using COO sparse format
  - Column-wise construction: for each state, iterate reactions
  - Off-diagonal entries: propensities of reactions leading to other states
  - Diagonal entries: negative sum of off-diagonals (maintains column sum = 0)
  - Returns triplet: `(A, in_flow, out_flow)`

- `reconstruct_generator()`: Incremental rebuild (optimization)
  - Reuses columns for states present in previous step (matched by global ID)
  - Builds new columns from scratch
  - Falls back to full rebuild if overlap < 30%

#### **5. `/home/adiden/DiscStochSim.jl/src/adaptive_fsp/problem.jl`**
**Purpose**: Problem definition
- `FSPProblem{E,T}` struct: encapsulates CME problem

  - `marginal()`: Get marginal distribution for one species at specific time

  2. **Build generator**: Construct CME matrix

- **System**: Robertson autocatalytic system (A→B, 2B→C+B, C+B→A+C)
- **Demonstrates**: Extreme stiffness handling (rates differ by ~1e7)
- **Parameters**: k1=0.04, k2=3e6, k3=1.0
- **Challenge**: Requires small time-steps (ε_dt=0.01) and tight flux tolerance

#### **4. `/home/adiden/DiscStochSim.jl/examples/bottleneck_paper_plots.jl`**
- **Purpose**: Generate figures for paper submission
- **Implements**: Explicit FSP loops (not using solve()) for fine-grained control
- **Outputs**: 
  - `flux_vs_naive_comparison.png` - comparing pruning strategies
  - `error_accumulation_analysis.png` - error over time
- **Advanced**: Uses `reconstruct_generator()` for efficiency

---

### Test Suite (`/home/adiden/DiscStochSim.jl/test/runtests.jl`)

Comprehensive test coverage:
1. **StateSpace basics**: add/remove/duplicate handling
2. **Renormalization**: probability normalization
3. **BoundaryCondition**: validation of domain checking
4. **DiscreteStochasticSystem**: Catalyst integration
5. **Generator column sums**: verifies CME mathematical property (column sum = 0)
6. **Reconstruction accuracy**: `reconstruct_generator()` matches `build_generator()`
7. **State expansion**: neighbor discovery
8. **FSP solve smoke test**: end-to-end integration test
9. **Marginal distributions**: probability distribution extraction

---

### Paper Materials (`/home/adiden/DiscStochSim.jl/paper/`)

Contains LaTeX manuscripts, responses to reviewers, and figures:
- **Main papers**: `ex_article.tex`, `backup.tex`, `docsiamart.pdf`
- **Supplementary**: `ex_supplement.tex`, `ex_shared.tex`
- **Reviewer responses**: `response.tex`, `response_round2.tex`, `reviewer_response.tex`
- **Figures**: EPS and PDF figures for simulation results, benchmarks, error analysis
- **References**: `references.bib` (bibliography)

---

### Key Algorithms & Concepts

#### **Quantile-Based Pruning**
1. Sort states by probability
2. Find cumulative probability threshold α
3. Remove all states below quantile with probability mass ≤ α
4. Renormalize remaining probabilities

#### **Flux-Aware Protection**
- Prevents removal of states with high outgoing probability flux
- Computes `flux[i] = p(x) * sum_k α_k(x)` (activity indicator)
- Only prunes candidates with flux below tolerance threshold
- Critical for bottleneck systems where rare states are essential for dynamics

#### **Adaptive Time-Stepping**
- Time step size inversely proportional to total probability flux
- `dt = ε_dt / total_flux` ensures stability
- Automatic scaling: high-flux regions → small steps; low-flux → large steps

#### **Incremental Generator Reconstruction**
- Reuse matrix columns when states persist across iterations
- Only rebuild columns for new/removed states
- Significant speedup for systems with slow state space evolution

---

### Dependencies & Imports

**Project Dependencies** (`Project.toml`):
- `Catalyst`: Chemical reaction network DSL
- `Expokit`: Matrix exponential computation (`expmv`)
- `CommonSolve`: Standard solver interface
- `LinearAlgebra`: Matrix operations
- `SparseArrays`: Sparse matrix support
- `Plots`, `UnicodePlots`: Visualization

---

```julia
       compress!, renormalize!, get_global_ids
export build_generator, reconstruct_generator
export FSPProblem, FSPSolution, AdaptiveFSP
export solve, mean_trajectory, marginal
```

---

### Summary

**DiscStochSim.jl** is a sophisticated numerical solver for discrete stochastic systems emphasizing:
- **Mathematical rigor**: Error bounds on truncation, proper CME discretization
- **Efficiency**: Incremental reconstruction, flux-aware pruning
- **Robustness**: Adaptive stepping, boundary conditions
- **Extensibility**: Clean separation of concerns (model, state space, generator, solver)
- **Validation**: Comprehensive tests and realistic examples

The implementation directly supports the associated research paper on flux-aware state space pruning for improved accuracy in chemical master equation solvers.

    30→\noindent Dear Editor and Reviewers,
    31→
    32→We thank the reviewers for their careful and constructive evaluation of our manuscript.
    33→In light of the reports, we have undertaken a major revision that changes both the
    34→scope and the technical core of the paper.
    35→
    36→The original submission focused on a \emph{quantile-based} pruning strategy: at each
    37→time step, a fixed fraction of probability mass was removed and the distribution was
    38→renormalized. As Reviewer~1 rightly pointed out, such probability-only pruning can
    39→fail badly in the presence of bottleneck reactions, and the error analysis in that
    40→version was not rigorous enough.
    41→
    42→In the revised manuscript we now present a \emph{flux-preserving adaptive FSP}
    43→framework whose central ideas are:
    44→
    45→\begin{enumerate}[topsep=0pt,itemsep=2pt]
    46→  \item Use \emph{probability flux}---rather than probability alone---to identify
    47→        states that are dynamically important but may be rarely occupied
    48→        (Definitions~3.1–3.2).
    49→  \item Combine quantile-based pruning with a \emph{flux safeguard} that prevents
    50→        the removal of low-probability, high-flux bottleneck states (Section~3.2
    51→        and Algorithm~3.1).
    52→  \item Drive the time-step selection by the \emph{total system flux}, leading to a
    53→        flux-adaptive time-step controller that automatically shortens the time
    54→        step during stiff or transient phases and enlarges it in slow regimes
    55→        (Corollary~4.8).
    56→  \item Derive a new error analysis based on a block-decomposed generator and
    57→        boundary fluxes, yielding rigorous local and global $\ell_1$ error bounds
    58→        via contraction of the stochastic semigroup (Section~4, especially
    59→        Proposition~4.1, Theorem~4.4, and Corollaries~4.6–4.8).
    60→  \item Demonstrate the algorithm on demanding benchmark problems, including a
    61→        bottleneck system, a stochastic toggle switch, the oscillatory Oregonator,
    62→        and the stiff Robertson (ROBER) autocatalytic system, with detailed
    63→        reporting of algorithmic parameters, state-space sizes, and performance
    64→        (Sections~3.3, 4.3, and~5).
    65→\end{enumerate}
    66→
    67→Below we respond point-by-point to the reviewers' comments.
    68→
    69→%======================================================================
    70→\section*{Response to Reviewer 1}
    71→%======================================================================
    72→
    73→\subsection*{Major Comments}
    74→
    75→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.1:} \textit{Lines 178–180: Can the authors elaborate why using a fixed probability
    76→cutoff ``can be unreliable when the overall probability distribution changes
    77→drastically over time''?}
    78→
    79→\textbf{Response:} We have considerably expanded both the explanation and the
    80→numerical evidence for this point.
    81→
    82→Conceptually, the difficulty is that low probability does not imply negligible
    83→dynamical importance: states with small $p(x,t)$ but large exit rates $w(x)$ can
    84→carry significant probability flux and act as essential conduits between regions of
    85→state space. This is now formalized in Definitions~3.1–3.2, where we define the
    86→outgoing probability flux
    87→\[
    88→  \Phi(x,t) = p(x,t)\,w(x)
    89→\]
    90→and the total system flux
    91→\[
    92→  \Phi_{\mathrm{total}}(J,t)
    93→  = \sum_{x\in J} \Phi(x,t),
    94→\]
    95→and we explicitly point out that such states can be connectivity-critical despite
    96→being rarely occupied (lines 148–156).
    97→
    98→To make this concrete, the revised Introduction and Section~3.3 now use the
    99→reviewer’s bottleneck idea:
   100→\[
   101→  A \xrightarrow{k_1} B, \qquad B \xrightarrow{k_2} B + C,
   102→\]
   103→with $k_1 \ll k_2$ and initial condition $(N_A,N_B,N_C) = (1,0,0)$. In this system
   104→the intermediate state with $(N_A,N_B)=(0,1)$ maintains very small probability but
   105→large exit flux, and it is the \emph{only} pathway to increasing $C$.
   106→
   107→Section~3.3 shows (Figure~3 and Table~1) that:
   108→
   109→\begin{itemize}
   110→  \item Under the original, probability-only pruning (quantile step without flux
   111→        safeguard), states on this bottleneck path are removed as soon as their
   112→        probability falls below the quantile threshold. This makes the truncated
   113→        generator reducible and effectively traps probability near $(1,0,0)$.
   114→  \item Under the new flux-preserving algorithm, the same states are protected
   115→        because their $\Phi(x,t)$ constitutes a non-negligible fraction of the
   116→        total system flux, even though $p(x,t)$ is tiny. As a result, the
   117→        algorithm correctly captures the transition to large $C$ and the advancing
   118→        probability wave front.
   119→\end{itemize}
   120→
   121→Thus the revised manuscript both explains and demonstrates why fixed probability
   122→cutoffs can be unreliable and how the flux safeguard resolves the failure mode.
   123→
   124→\vspace{0.5em}
   125→
   126→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.2:} \textit{Is it necessary to always renormalize the generator matrix and the
   127→probability distribution? One powerful property of FSP comes from controlling
   128→the loss of probability mass via $1-\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{p}(t)$. Also, if the
   129→truncated generator is simply the principal submatrix of the full generator and
   130→is never renormalized, then $1-\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{p}(t)$ is a global error
   131→estimate. Can the authors elaborate why normalization is favorable or necessary
   132→and why their more elaborate error control is better?}
   133→
   134→\textbf{Response:} We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. The
   135→revised manuscript clarifies the distinction between \emph{generator} normalization
   136→and \emph{probability} normalization, and explains how our flux-based error control
   137→relates to the classical FSP bound.
   138→
   139→\begin{itemize}
   140→  \item \emph{Generator:} In the revised method we \emph{do not} renormalize the
   141→        generator. Instead, Section~4.1 constructs a \emph{compressed generator}
   142→        $A_{JJ}$ on the active set $J$ by folding transitions into and out of
   143→        the complement $J'$ into a reflecting boundary term (equation~(4.4)). As
   144→        shown in Proposition~4.1, this compressed generator satisfies
   145→        $\mathbf{1}^\top A_{JJ} = 0$ and hence generates a contraction
   146→        semigroup in $\ell_1$. This is conceptually similar to taking a principal
   147→        submatrix but retains the effect of the truncated region through the
   148→        boundary term.
   149→
   150→  \item \emph{Probability:} The probability vector on $J$ is renormalized after
   151→        each pruning event so that $\|\mathbf{p}_J(t_n)\|_1 = 1$ holds at the
   152→        discrete times $t_n$. This keeps the numerical solution interpretable as
   153→        a probability distribution on the current active set and improves
   154→        numerical robustness when the remaining mass is small. In the error
   155→        analysis, the renormalization contribution is explicitly accounted for in
   156→        the local model error and is bounded by the pruned mass.
   157→
   158→  \item \emph{Relation to $1-\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{p}_J(t)$:} For a fixed FSP
   159→        with generator equal to a principal submatrix of the full generator,
   160→        $1-\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{p}_J(t)$ indeed bounds the probability that has
   161→        left $J$. Our block-partitioned analysis in Section~4 recovers this view in
   162→        more detail. In Theorem~4.4 we express the local model error over a time
   163→        step $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$ in terms of the \emph{boundary fluxes}
   164→        $\Phi_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{in}}$ between $J$ and $J'$. Then
   165→        Corollary~4.6 shows that the global error after $N$ steps satisfies
   166→        \[
   167→          e_N \le \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (\varepsilon_n + \tau_n),
   168→        \]
   169→        where $\varepsilon_n$ is an integral of these boundary fluxes and $\tau_n$
   170→        is the numerical time-stepping error.
   171→\end{itemize}
   172→
   173→Compared to a single scalar quantity $1-\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{p}_J(t)$, the
   174→flux-based decomposition distinguishes (i) model error due to truncation and
   175→pruning (through boundary fluxes and pruned mass) from (ii) numerical error due to
   176→the matrix exponential. This structure directly motivates our adaptive strategy,
   177→which uses the boundary fluxes to decide when to expand the state space and how to
   178→adjust the time step. We have added a short remark in Section~4.2 to make this
   179→connection explicit.
   180→
   181→\vspace{0.5em}
   182→
   183→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.3:} \textit{The proof for Theorem 3.10 is incomplete. Specifically, I do not
   184→understand why the errors could simply be summed over the $N$ time steps.}
   185→
   186→\textbf{Response:} We agree that the previous argument was incomplete. In the revised
   187→manuscript, the old Theorem~3.10 has been removed and replaced by a new error
   188→analysis in Section~4, culminating in Corollary~4.6 (global error bound).
   189→
   190→The revised analysis proceeds as follows:
   191→
   192→\begin{itemize}
   193→  \item Proposition~4.1 proves that the compressed generator $A_{JJ}$ generates a
   194→        contraction semigroup in $\ell_1$, i.e.,
   195→        $\|\mathrm{e}^{A_{JJ} t}\|_{1\to 1} = 1$ for $t\ge 0$.
   196→  \item Theorem~4.4 bounds the \emph{local model error} over one time step in terms
   197→        of the integrated boundary fluxes across the truncation.
   198→  \item Proposition~4.5 bounds the \emph{local time-stepping error} for the
   199→        Krylov-based matrix exponential approximation, controlled by the ODE
   200→        tolerance $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ODE}}$.
   201→  \item Corollary~4.6 then combines these pieces to show that
   202→        \[
   203→          e_{n+1} \le e_n + \varepsilon_n + \tau_n,
   204→        \]
   205→        and by induction
   206→        \[
   207→          e_N \le \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (\varepsilon_n + \tau_n),
   208→        \]
   209→        where $e_n$ is the global $\ell_1$ error at time $t_n$.
   210→\end{itemize}
   211→
   212→Because the semigroup is contractive, local errors do \emph{not} get amplified as
   213→they are propagated forward in time, which justifies the additive accumulation in
   214→Corollary~4.6. We now make this point explicit in the proof.
   215→
   216→\vspace{0.5em}
   217→
   218→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.4:} \textit{Certain fringe models with “bottleneck reactions” might be nontrivial
   219→with any FSP with time-stepping or sliding windows, including the method in this
   220→paper. [A specific three-species bottleneck system is described and the reviewer
   221→asks the authors to comment.]}
   222→
   223→\textbf{Response:} We are very grateful for this comment; it directly motivated one of
   224→the central case studies in the revised manuscript.
   225→
   226→Section~3.3 now presents a detailed bottleneck example closely following the
   227→reviewer’s suggestion. We consider a three-species system with a slow activation step
   228→and a fast production step leading to an advancing front in $C$. The parameters are
   229→chosen so that the intermediate states on the activation path have extremely low
   230→probability but carry the only significant flux into regions with large $C$.
   231→
   232→In this setting we compare:
   233→
   234→\begin{itemize}
   235→  \item a probability-only variant (quantile pruning without flux safeguard), and
   236→  \item the full flux-preserving algorithm (Algorithm~3.1 combined with the
   237→        flux-adaptive time stepping of Section~3.2).
   238→\end{itemize}
   239→
   240→Figure~3 and Table~1 show that the probability-only variant quickly removes
   241→bottleneck states from the truncated set, after which the numerical solution remains
   242→localized near the initial state and fails to reproduce the growth of $C$. In
   243→contrast, the flux-preserving variant retains bottleneck states whenever their exit
   244→flux remains a non-negligible fraction of the total system flux, and it reproduces
   245→the expected increase in $\langle C\rangle$ over several orders of magnitude in time.
   246→The example thus illustrates precisely the kind of pathology the reviewer described
   247→and demonstrates that the flux safeguard is effective in protecting such bottleneck
   248→channels.
   249→
   250→\vspace{0.5em}
   251→
   252→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.5:} \textit{Can the authors compare their method to previous FSP methods that
   253→also incorporate adaptive state spaces, either in discussion or numerical tests?
   254→Some are already cited in the paper. Another paper that comes to mind is Dinh \&
   255→Sidje (Physical Biology, 2017).}
   256→
   257→\textbf{Response:} We have expanded the discussion of related work in the
   258→Introduction and in Section~2.3 to position the revised method more clearly among
   259→existing approaches.
   260→
   261→In particular, we now discuss:
   262→
   263→\begin{itemize}
   264→  \item \emph{Aggregation and lumping methods} such as those of Bobbio \& Trivedi and
   265→        Zhang, Watson, \& Cao, which group micro-states into macro-states using
   266→        stationary or Monte Carlo information. These methods achieve substantial
   267→        reduction but rely on either a priori timescale separation or sufficiently
   268→        rich sampling.
   269→  \item \emph{Sliding-window and hybrid FSP–SSA schemes} such as those by Wolf
   270→        et al.\ and MacNamara et al., which track moving regions of support or
   271→        combine deterministic and stochastic updates.
   272→  \item \emph{Krylov-FSP-SSA and tensor-train methods} of Dinh \& Sidje and
   273→        collaborators, which guide state-space expansion using SSA trajectories or
   274→        compressed representations (as cited in references [6–7]).
   275→\end{itemize}
   276→
   277→Our flux-preserving adaptive FSP differs in two main ways:
   278→
   279→\begin{enumerate}
   280→  \item We use \emph{absolute boundary flux} as the main control quantity, which
   281→        leads directly to the local and global error bounds in Section~4, rather
   282→        than relying on relative flux thresholds or stationary information.
   283→  \item We decouple discovery of new states (via reachability expansion of the
   284→        reaction network) from the pruning decision, using quantiles only as a
   285→        pre-selection mechanic and flux as the final safeguard. This explicitly
   286→        addresses the bottleneck scenario highlighted by the reviewer.
   287→\end{enumerate}
   288→
   289→Implementing and tuning several competing adaptive FSP codes for a full numerical
   290→benchmark on all our examples would require a substantial additional effort and is
   291→beyond the scope of the current revision. Instead we focus on clearly articulating
   292→the conceptual differences, and we hope the detailed algorithmic description and
   293→performance data in the revised manuscript will facilitate future comparisons by
   294→other groups.
   295→
   296→\vspace{0.5em}
   297→
   298→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.6:} \textit{Although well studied, Michaelis–Menten, Lotka–Volterra, and toggle
   299→switch models are relatively simple to solve. It would be beneficial to showcase
   300→your algorithm with at least one example where the state space is known to be
   301→large. Can the authors implement such a model?}
   302→
   303→\textbf{Response:} We agree that more demanding examples are needed to demonstrate the
   304→advantages of the method. The revised manuscript contains several such systems.
   305→
   306→\begin{itemize}
   307→  \item Section~5.1 revisits the stochastic toggle switch, but now primarily as a
   308→        qualitative illustration of bistability and basin switching under the
   309→        flux-preserving truncation (Figure~6).
   310→  \item Section~5.2 introduces the \textbf{Oregonator} model of chemical
   311→        oscillations. The natural bounding box for the molecular copy numbers has
   312→        on the order of $3\times 10^7$ states, whereas the adaptive FSP keeps
   313→        between a few hundred and a few thousand states active at any time,
   314→        achieving a compression ratio of roughly $10^4:1$ while faithfully
   315→        reproducing the oscillatory dynamics (Figure~7).
   316→  \item Section~5.3 adds the \textbf{Robertson (ROBER) autocatalytic system}, which
   317→        is extremely stiff, with reaction rates spanning nine orders of magnitude.
   318→        A conservative rectangular bounding box guided by the mean trajectories
   319→        would contain on the order of $10^8$–$10^9$ states, whereas the adaptive
   320→        state space in our simulations remains in the range $50$--$2000$ states.
   321→        Thus the method achieves a compression of several orders of magnitude
   322→        while still capturing the three-phase dynamics (slow initiation, explosive
   323→        autocatalysis, and long equilibration) and controlling local boundary flux
   324→        and time-stepping error (Figure~8 and Table~5).
   325→
   326→\end{itemize}
   327→
   328→These examples go beyond the original low-dimensional tests and show that the
   329→flux-preserving adaptive FSP can handle genuinely large and stiff systems.

   347→\subsection*{Main Comments}
   348→
   349→\noindent\textbf{Comment 2.1:} \textit{The first experiment, depicted in Figure 2, requires a much deeper
   350→discussion. The error seems to increase with time, contradicting the analysis.
   351→Also, 1000 SSA trajectories would not be enough to eliminate statistical error.}
   352→
   353→\textbf{Response:} We agree that the original SSA-based experiment did not clearly
   354→separate truncation error from Monte Carlo sampling error, and that the discussion
   355→of error growth was incomplete.
   356→
   357→In the revised manuscript we have \emph{replaced} this experiment by a deterministic
   358→error study that directly tests the theoretical results:
   359→
   360→\begin{itemize}
   361→  \item Section~4.3 (\emph{Experimental Error Analysis}) compares the
   362→        flux-preserving adaptive FSP to a high-accuracy fixed-FSP reference on a
   363→        bounded state space $\{0,\dots,2\}\times\{0,\dots,2\}\times\{0,\dots,10000\}$.
   364→  \item Figure~5 shows that the relative error in $\langle C\rangle$ remains below
   365→        $0.1\%$ and decreases to about $0.015\%$ as the distribution spreads
   366→        (panel~5a). The instantaneous error rate is approximately constant at
   367→        $4.9\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ (panel~5b), in agreement with the
   368→        additive error structure of Corollary~4.6. Panel~5d confirms linear
   369→        scaling of the absolute error with $\langle C\rangle$, corresponding to
   370→        about $0.01\%$ relative error over three orders of magnitude in
   371→        population.
   372→  \item Table~2 reports final-time means and errors for all species at $t=10^5$~s,
   373→        with the adaptive and reference solutions in close agreement and the
   374→        adaptive state space about $4.5$ times smaller than the fixed one.
   375→\end{itemize}
   376→
   377→We believe this new experiment more directly and transparently validates the
   378→revised error analysis.
   379→
   380→\vspace{0.5em}
   381→
   382→\noindent\textbf{Comment 2.2:} \textit{For most (if not all) experiments, the pruning factor $\alpha$, the
   383→effective pruned fraction $m$, and the time step are not reported. These should
   384→be specified in the paper rather than needing to be inferred from the code.}
   385→
   386→\textbf{Response:} We have revised the numerical sections to state the key algorithmic
   387→parameters explicitly:
   388→
   389→\begin{itemize}
   390→  \item Section~3.3, which introduces the flux-preserving pruning algorithm, now
   391→        specifies the quantile tolerance $\alpha$, flux tolerance $\varepsilon_{\rm
   392→        flux}$, and the bounds $\Delta t_{\min}$ and $\Delta t_{\max}$ used in the
   393→        bottleneck experiments, as well as the functional form of the flux-based
   394→        time-step rule.
   395→  \item Section~4.3 provides the time grid and state-space bounds for the fixed-FSP
   396→        reference solution, and the adaptive time-step settings for the comparison
   397→        run.
   398→  \item Sections~5.1–5.3 state the choices of $\alpha$, flux tolerance, and
   399→        time-step range used in the toggle, Oregonator, and ROBER examples. The
   400→        figures also show the resulting adaptive time steps and state-space sizes
   401→        as functions of time.
   402→\end{itemize}
   403→
   404→In the revised method, $\alpha$ primarily determines how much probability mass is
   405→\emph{eligible} for pruning per step, while the flux safeguard further constrains
   406→which of those states can actually be removed. Rather than reporting an effective
   407→$m$ at every time step, we focus on how $\alpha$, the flux threshold, and the
   408→boundary fluxes enter the local and global error bounds in Section~4.
   409→
   410→\vspace{0.5em}
   411→
   412→\noindent\textbf{Comment 2.3:} \textit{I would like to see more explicitly the relation between the pruning
   413→factor $\alpha$ and the effective pruned fraction $m$. This relationship will
   414→affect both efficiency and accuracy.}
   415→
   416→\textbf{Response:} We appreciate this request and have clarified the role of $\alpha$
   417→in the revised algorithm.
   418→
   419→In the original quantile-only scheme, $\alpha$ directly controlled the fraction of
   420→probability mass removed at each pruning step, so $m \approx \alpha$. The new
   421→method introduces an additional flux-based safeguard:
   422→
   423→\begin{itemize}
   424→  \item The quantile parameter $\alpha$ selects a \emph{candidate set} of low-probability
   425→        states whose cumulative probability does not exceed $\alpha$.
   426→  \item The flux safeguard then scans this candidate set and retains any state
   427→        whose outgoing flux exceeds a prescribed fraction of the total system flux.
   428→        These protected states are not pruned, regardless of their probability.
   429→\end{itemize}
   430→
   431→As a consequence, the \emph{effective} pruned mass $m$ is at most $\alpha$, and can
   432→be considerably smaller when bottleneck states are present. This behavior is
   433→illustrated in the bottleneck experiment: even with a relatively large $\alpha$, the
   434→flux safeguard prevents removal of the intermediate bottleneck states and thereby
   435→limits $m$ while maintaining connectivity. Equation~(4.22) and the discussion in
   436→Section~4.2 make explicit how the local model error depends on the pruned mass, the
   437→boundary fluxes, and the time step, thereby connecting $\alpha$ and $m$ through
   438→their impact on the flux-based error control.
   439→
   440→A full parametric study of $(\alpha,m)$ over many systems would significantly
   441→lengthen the paper; we therefore leave a more systematic investigation of this
   442→relationship to future work.
   443→
   444→\vspace{0.5em}
   445→
   446→\noindent\textbf{Comment 2.4:} \textit{The authors report runtimes for their new algorithm, but these are
   447→only average values on a single hardware platform. At least the hardware used
   448→should be mentioned, and runtimes should be compared to those of existing
   449→algorithms; probably higher-dimensional examples need to be studied as well.}
   450→
   451→\textbf{Response:} We agree that performance information and reproducibility are
   452→important. In the revised manuscript we have:
   453→
   454→\begin{itemize}
   455→    \item Specified the implementation details and hardware in Section~4.1: all
   456→        experiments were run in Julia using Expokit.jl for Krylov-based matrix
   457→        exponential computations, Catalyst.jl for reaction-network modeling, and
   458→        sparse matrix structures from the \texttt{SparseArrays} standard library.
   459→        Simulations were performed on a MacBook Pro with an M1 Pro chip and
   460→        32\,GB of RAM.
   461→  \item Added Section~6 and Section~6.1, which analyze the performance of the
   462→        \emph{matrix reconstruction} strategy that reuses generator entries when
   463→        consecutive active state spaces overlap. Figure~9 and Table~6 show that,
   464→        for the Oregonator model, reconstruction reduces the median time for
   465→        generator construction from about $19.2$~ms to $1.25$~ms, a speedup of
   466→        roughly $15\times$ at the kernel level. Figure~10 and Table~7 then report
   467→        total simulation times, where matrix reconstruction yields speedups of
   468→        about $3.9\times$ (Oregonator), $3.5\times$ (ROBER), and $2.9\times$
   469→        (toggle switch) relative to a standard implementation that rebuilds the
   470→        matrix from scratch at each time step.
   471→\end{itemize}
   472→
   473→A direct head-to-head comparison with all existing adaptive FSP implementations
   474→(e.g., Optimal FSP, Krylov-FSP-SSA, aggregation-based methods) on the same
   475→hardware would require reimplementing or interfacing with multiple external codes,
   476→and carefully tuning each method for fairness. We believe this is an interesting
   477→direction for future work but beyond the scope of the present revision. Our goal
   478→here is to document the internal performance characteristics of the proposed
   479→algorithm and to provide enough detail for readers to compare against their own
   480→implementations.
   481→
   482→\vspace{0.5em}
   483→
   484→\noindent\textbf{Comment 2.5:} \textit{Include a test case where excessive pruning would be an issue but
   485→your new method avoids that problem.}
   486→
